<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Shuai Shao
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Kangning Zhang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Qingyao Li
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Shijian Wang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Hao Wang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">
<br class="ltx_break">Wenxiang Jiao
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yuan Lu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yi Guo
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Weiwen Liu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Weinan Zhang
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Agents built around large language models continually accumulate interaction trajectories during deployment, yet their behavior typically remains fixed.
Beyond updating model weights, these trajectories can improve the agent harness that constructs context, mediates tools, validates actions, and recovers execution.
We introduce Harness-R1, the first method, to our knowledge, that makes failure-conditioned, lifecycle-wide editing of an existing executable runtime a learned capability. It post-trains a dedicated harness engineer with online reinforcement learning so that its edits are optimized for the realized task success they produce, rather than proposed by a fixed editor.
A separate 9B engineer converts batches of target-agent failures into validated executable patches; fresh same-batch reruns of the frozen target provide outcome rewards, so training updates only the engineer.
Cold-start supervised fine-tuning initializes this editing policy, which is then trained online with group-relative policy optimization.
Across WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench, Harness-R1 raises vanilla Qwen3.5-9B success from 44.3% to 53.6% (<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+9.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>9.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+9.3</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points).
After direct target-agent fine-tuning, a target-specific engineer raises the average further from 59.2% to 64.2% (<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+5.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>5.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+5.0</annotation></semantics></math> points); because these gains hold both before and after fine-tuning the target, Harness-R1 points toward co-evolving the harness engineer and the target agent.</p>
  
</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliation"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliation: </span>Shanghai Jiao Tong University</span></span></span><span id="id2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliation"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliation: </span>Xiaohongshu Inc.</span></span></span><span id="id3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliation"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliation: </span>Southeast University</span></span></span><span id="id4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_contribution"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">contribution: </span>Work done during internship at Xiaohongshu Inc.</span></span></span><span id="id5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_contribution"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">contribution: </span>Equal contribution</span></span></span><span id="id6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_contribution"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">contribution: </span>Corresponding authors</span></span></span><span id="id7" class="ltx_note"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">: </span><span id="id7.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-0.8pt;">

<span id="id9.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:18.7pt;height:6.4pt;vertical-align:-0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-0.8pt,0.3pt) scale(0.9,0.9) ;">

</span>
</span></span></span> Models: <a href="https://huggingface.co/ShaoShuai0605/Harness-R1" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/ShaoShuai0605/Harness-R1</a></span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models serve as the decision core of tool-using agents, enabling them to interpret tasks, maintain state, and pursue complex goals through multi-turn interaction with external environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>)</cite>.
Unlike a single model invocation, a deployed agent continually produces trajectories containing observations, actions, environment feedback, and task outcomes.
These trajectories record successful experience, but they also expose systematic failures such as tool misuse, lost state, protocol violations, repeated attempts, and failed recovery.
This raises a natural question: can agents use their interaction experience to improve continually rather than remain fixed after deployment?
This experience-to-improvement loop is a central concern of self-evolving agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">An agent system can improve at two complementary locations.
One line updates model parameters through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or online learning, directly improving the actor that makes task decisions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>)</cite>.
The other keeps the model fixed and optimizes the <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">agent harness</em> around it.
Context construction, memory and skills, tool mediation, action validation, and control and recovery logic are all harness components <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>)</cite>.
Together, they determine what the model observes, which actions it can execute, how it interprets environment feedback, and how execution recovers after deviations.
Identical model weights can therefore yield substantially different agent capabilities under different harnesses.
Harness optimization offers a complementary path to model training: it improves the runtime mechanisms between a model and its environment without changing the model itself.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.02276v1/FIG_motivation_editing.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="286" height="159"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Matched-baseline reward changes across three benchmarks; diamonds denote the equal-weight average.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Direct harness modification is not uniformly reliable.
Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> compares matched-baseline changes in mean environment reward across the three benchmarks.
A fixed Self-Refine rule <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>)</cite> lowers reward on all three benchmarks, and the gains from frontier harness editors are unstable or limited, with some even reducing the WebShop reward.
Prompting strong but fixed models to edit the harness is therefore not reliable enough.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond such prompted edits, recent systems build dedicated harness-optimization pipelines.
Meta-Harness, Agentic Harness Engineering, and AutoHarness use agentic proposers to jointly edit prompts, tools, memory, middleware, or control logic from harness state, execution traces, and task feedback; Life-Harness and HarnessX extend the editable surface to lifecycle interventions and typed components <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>)</cite>.
Yet the harness proposer usually remains fixed: outcomes select or iteratively refine patches without directly updating proposer parameters; HarnessX uses cross-harness GRPO to train the task model, while AEGIS retains symbolic harness editing.
Complementary work optimizes prompts, demonstrations, memories, skills, or task-solving programs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>)</cite>, but typically isolates one artifact or constructs a new solution program.
A workflow may be part of a harness, but generating one differs from learning to install failure-conditioned executable interventions into an existing multi-stage runtime.
The latter must decide when to intervene from actual target-agent failures and coordinate context, state, action execution, and recovery.
This leaves a less studied question: can we post-train a dedicated harness engineer with online reinforcement learning, so that improving an existing executable runtime from observed failures becomes a learned capability?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Training a harness engineer directly poses two challenges.
First, the editable runtime spans interdependent execution stages, so unrestricted code edits can break existing interfaces, produce non-executable behavior, or introduce changes unrelated to task success.
Second, text form and static rules cannot determine patch quality; only the target agent’s behavior after applying the patch can do so.
Training therefore requires a grounded feedback path from target-agent failures, through constrained executable edits, to the performance gain that updates the engineer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce Harness-R1, a training paradigm that post-trains a dedicated harness engineer with online reinforcement learning while keeping the target agent frozen.
Conditioned on batches of target-agent failures, the engineer generates validated executable runtime patches; the patched target reruns the same tasks, and the realized performance change rewards only the engineer.
Cold-start supervised fine-tuning initializes the policy before online GRPO.
Across WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench, Harness-R1 raises average success from 44.3% to 53.6% (<math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+9.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>9.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+9.3</annotation></semantics></math> points) for the vanilla target and from 59.2% to 64.2% (<math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+5.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>5.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+5.0</annotation></semantics></math> points) after direct target-agent fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The main contributions can be summarized as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formulate failure-conditioned, lifecycle-wide harness editing as an online reinforcement-learning problem for a dedicated engineer while keeping the target agent frozen.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We develop Harness-R1, combining cold-start supervised fine-tuning with group-relative policy optimization over the realized utility of executable runtime patches, and it improves the vanilla target by 9.3 points across three interactive benchmarks.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that the harness engineer and the target agent can co-evolve: after direct target-agent fine-tuning, a target-specific Harness-R1 engineer adds a further 5.0 points.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2608.02276v1/x1.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="476" height="244" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of Harness-R1. Mined target failures become an evidence bundle (left); the harness engineer writes an executable patch that edits four lifecycle points in the runtime surrounding the frozen target (right); the patched target reruns the same tasks, and the resulting same-batch reward trains only the engineer via cold-start SFT and then GRPO (bottom loop). See the Method section for the loop, action space, and lifecycle hooks.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM-Based Harness Evolution.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work treats the agent harness as an executable, multi-component optimization object.
One line searches or synthesizes whole harnesses from execution traces, evaluation scores, and rewards: Meta-Harness has a coding agent search over prior candidates, AutoHarness iteratively synthesizes code harnesses from environment-validity feedback, and AHE jointly evolves prompts, tools, middleware, skills, sub-agents, and memory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>)</cite>.
A second line turns recurring interaction failures into scoped, regression-checked repairs across multiple execution stages, combining trace-grounded diagnosis with regression-aware validation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>)</cite>.
As a closely related concurrent direction, HarnessX composes typed processors, performs symbolic trace-driven adaptation with AEGIS, and applies cross-harness GRPO to the task model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>)</cite>.
Across these systems the proposer may be a stronger external model or the target model itself, but none post-trains the proposer or editor weights from harness-editing outcomes; feedback instead guides program search, candidate selection, regression testing, or artifact promotion.
Harness-R1 instead moves the learning target from the resulting harness to the editing policy: online reinforcement learning post-trains a dedicated harness engineer from the realized utility of its patches on a frozen target agent.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Algorithmic Optimization of Harness Components.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A broader line optimizes prompts and other model-external artifacts within prespecified edit spaces and search procedures.
Some methods have an LLM propose and search over instruction candidates against a score, as in APE and OPRO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>)</cite>.
Others form natural-language “gradients” or textual feedback and propagate them to edit prompts or code, as in ProTeGi and TextGrad <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>)</cite>.
Population-based methods such as EvoPrompt, Promptbreeder, and GEPA mutate and select prompts by fitness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>)</cite>, whereas pipeline compilers such as DSPy and MIPRO separate program structure from module parameters and search over instructions and bootstrapped demonstrations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>)</cite>.
These methods can invoke strong language models and maintain histories, populations, or learned surrogates, but they generally do not post-train the proposer, reflector, or backward engine from editing outcomes; even when some fine-tune task modules, the product is a task-specific artifact or parameter rather than a dedicated harness-editor policy trained by editing outcomes.
Harness-R1 instead trains the editor from the realized execution effects of its patches and modifies multiple stages of an existing target-agent runtime.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Learned Harness Editors.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">More directly related work post-trains policies that edit or control model-external structures, but each either restricts the edit space or couples editing with task solving.
Some train a dedicated editor from downstream outcomes over a narrow target, such as an independent context field or a revisable skill bank <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>)</cite>, or learn to generate task-solving workflows run by a frozen executor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>)</cite>.
Closer to the runtime harness, others instruction-tune observation and action projections without reinforcement learning or persistent code patches, select among a few predefined structural actions under offline RL, or fold harness edits into a single task actor’s action space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>)</cite>.
In contrast, Harness-R1 isolates harness editing as a learning problem in its own right, casting failure-conditioned, lifecycle-wide editing as a standalone online reinforcement-learning task for a dedicated engineer, trained from the realized task outcomes of its executable patches while the target agent stays frozen.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we introduce Harness-R1, an online, outcome-grounded framework that post-trains a dedicated engineer to improve the executable runtime surrounding a frozen target agent.
We first formulate harness editing as a batch-conditioned learning problem in which each modification is evaluated by rerunning the same tasks.
We then describe where the modification can intervene across the agent lifecycle and how cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO learns the editing policy.
Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes this failure-to-edit-to-rerun loop and the separation between the trainable engineer and the frozen task agent.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> denote a frozen target agent (its model together with the surrounding base runtime), and let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> be a batch of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> tasks in environment <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>.
Within an episode the agent interacts with the environment over multiple turns: at each turn it reads the accumulated history and the current observation, and its frozen policy proposes an action.
Actions are expressed in the environment’s native interface: structured tool or API calls and textual commands, such as <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">search</span> and <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">click</span> in WebShop, navigation and object manipulation in ALFWorld, and SQL queries in DBBench.
The environment executes the action, returns the next observation, and emits an outcome reward once the episode ends.
The component we adapt is the base runtime: the code that assembles the context shown to the model, forwards each action to the environment, and relays the feedback back to the agent.
This surrounding runtime, and not the model’s weights, is exactly what the harness edits.
Running the unmodified agent over the batch yields baseline trajectories <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{i}^{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{i}^{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and rewards <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{i}^{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{i}^{0}</annotation></semantics></math>.
A deterministic extractor retains only failed episodes and compacts their task constraints, selected action–observation excerpts, outcomes, and necessary environment state into a failure packet <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{B}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The engineer <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> reads this packet once and generates a batch-conditioned executable overlay <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>; it neither answers the tasks nor participates in their rollouts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The overlay <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> wraps this loop as executable hooks at four lifecycle points, leaving the agent’s weights untouched (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, right): (i) <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">episode initialization</em> sets up the starting context and episode state; (ii) <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pre-decision</em> augments the context with retrieved guidance and interface constraints before the agent decides; (iii) <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pre-action</em> is a runtime guardrail that may canonicalize, rewrite, or veto the proposed action before it reaches the environment; and (iv) <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">post-feedback</em> inspects the returned observation and triggers recovery when the trajectory stalls.
These hooks thus touch only the inputs and outputs surrounding the frozen policy, never the policy itself, and patches are validated before installation, with invalid patches having no effect.
Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Executable Patch Interface ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> gives the invocation point and the permitted return effect of each hook.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">After validation, the overlay is installed and the same frozen target reruns every task in <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>, including tasks that originally succeeded.
Let <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{i}^{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>P</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{i}^{P}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the resulting reward.
Define the full-batch performance difference and the engineer reward as</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E1X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\Delta_{B}(P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\Delta_{B}(P)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(R_{i}^{P}-R_{i}^{0}\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>P</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(R_{i}^{P}-R_{i}^{0}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E1Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle r(B,P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle r(B,P)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\Delta_{B}(P),&amp;\text{if valid and complete},\\
0,&amp;\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>if valid and complete</mtext><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>otherwise</mtext><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\Delta_{B}(P),&amp;\text{if valid and complete},\\
0,&amp;\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">Using the same tasks before and after editing controls task composition but defines a same-batch, transductive objective, with no iterative refinement within an instance or persistent patch memory across batches.
This reward is non-differentiable and observable only after an edit changes target-agent behavior, so it cannot be optimized directly.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Outcome-Grounded Post-Training</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Harness-R1 learns the editing policy in two stages.
Cold-start supervised fine-tuning first initializes a prior over valid, executable edits, and online, outcome-grounded GRPO then optimizes the realized task utility of patches applied to the frozen target.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cold-start supervised fine-tuning.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first run the frozen target with its base harness and form editing instances from the resulting failed trajectories.
The teacher and RL instances use disjoint task batches.
A strong teacher proposes serialized editing responses <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{j}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{j}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> from the compact failure packets <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>; we validate and evaluate their parsed overlays with the frozen target, retaining at most one executable, complete, non-regressive response per packet.
The resulting dataset <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=\{(s_{j},y_{j}^{T})\}_{j=1}^{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>SFT</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=\{(s_{j},y_{j}^{T})\}_{j=1}^{M}</annotation></semantics></math> initializes the engineer by teacher-forced next-token prediction:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)&amp;=-\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}|y_{j}^{T}|}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{j}^{T}|}\\[-2.0pt]
&amp;\quad\log H_{\theta}\!\left(y_{j,t}^{T}\mid s_{j},y_{j,&lt;t}^{T}\right).\end{aligned}\hskip 11.99998pt" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>SFT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>M</mi></msup><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mspace style="width:1.2em;" width="1.2em"></mspace></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)&amp;=-\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}|y_{j}^{T}|}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{j}^{T}|}\\[-2.0pt]
&amp;\quad\log H_{\theta}\!\left(y_{j,t}^{T}\mid s_{j},y_{j,&lt;t}^{T}\right).\end{aligned}\hskip 11.99998pt</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Outcome-grounded GRPO.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Starting from the supervised policy, we perform online GRPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>)</cite> and sample <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=8</annotation></semantics></math> candidate patches from the current policy for each failure packet (Alg. <a href="#algorithm1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Outcome-grounded GRPO. ‣ 3.2 Outcome-Grounded Post-Training ‣ 3 Method ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, lines 4–5).
Each candidate is parsed and validated into a patch (line 6); each valid patch is then installed independently and evaluated by rerunning the frozen target on the same full task batch (line 7), while invalid, no-op, or incomplete evaluations receive zero reward under Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.1 Problem Setup ‣ 3 Method ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) (line 8).
For rewards <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{k}=r(B,P_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{k}=r(B,P_{k})</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{B}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{B}</annotation></semantics></math> be the empirical mean and standard deviation within the eight candidates generated from the same packet, and normalize the rewards into advantages (line 10):</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{A}_{k}=\frac{r_{k}-\mu_{B}}{\sigma_{B}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{A}_{k}=\frac{r_{k}-\mu_{B}}{\sigma_{B}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{k}=(y_{k,1},\ldots,y_{k,T_{k}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{k}=(y_{k,1},\ldots,y_{k,T_{k}})</annotation></semantics></math> be the engineer response parsed into <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, and let
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{k,t}(\theta)=H_{\theta}(y_{k,t}\mid s_{B},y_{k,&lt;t})/H_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{k,t}\mid s_{B},y_{k,&lt;t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>old</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{k,t}(\theta)=H_{\theta}(y_{k,t}\mid s_{B},y_{k,&lt;t})/H_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{k,t}\mid s_{B},y_{k,&lt;t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The sequence-level advantage is shared by all response tokens, and the engineer maximizes the token-averaged clipped surrogate</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E4X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle g_{k,t}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle g_{k,t}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\min\!\Big\{\rho_{k,t}\widehat{A}_{k}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mpadded style="width:1.653em;" width="1.653em"><mi>min</mi></mpadded><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>ρ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\min\!\Big\{\rho_{k,t}\widehat{A}_{k},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="3" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E4Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{k,t},1-\epsilon_{\ell},1+\epsilon_{h})\widehat{A}_{k}\Big\}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>clip</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ρ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{k,t},1-\epsilon_{\ell},1+\epsilon_{h})\widehat{A}_{k}\Big\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E4Xb" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4Xb.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒥</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4Xb.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{T_{k}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{k}}w_{k,t}g_{k,t}(\theta)\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></munderover></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{T_{k}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{k}}w_{k,t}g_{k,t}(\theta)\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.4" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\mathrm{tr}}_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>tr</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\mathrm{tr}}_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\mathrm{ro}}_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>ro</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\mathrm{ro}}_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math> are the old-policy token log probabilities recomputed by the training engine and recorded by the rollout engine, respectively; <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{k,t}=\operatorname{clip}(\exp(\ell^{\mathrm{tr}}_{k,t}-\ell^{\mathrm{ro}}_{k,t}),0,2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>clip</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>tr</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>ro</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{k,t}=\operatorname{clip}(\exp(\ell^{\mathrm{tr}}_{k,t}-\ell^{\mathrm{ro}}_{k,t}),0,2)</annotation></semantics></math> is the truncated importance weight.
WebShop supplies shaped environment reward, whereas ALFWorld and DBBench supply binary success; no format-validity bonus or explicit KL loss is added.
Only the engineer parameters <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> are updated (line 12), and the outer loop iterates over update bundles until the training budget is exhausted (lines 2 and 13).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Algorithm <a href="#algorithm1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Outcome-grounded GRPO. ‣ 3.2 Outcome-Grounded Post-Training ‣ 3 Method ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the online RL stage.
Base trajectories, rewards, and failure packets are cached before optimization; online evaluation reruns only the patched target for candidates sampled from the current engineer.</p>
</div>
<figure id="algorithm1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="algorithm1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Online RL for harness editing.</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate Harness-R1 on three interactive environments that stress different forms of agent execution.
We ask whether outcome-trained harness editing improves over supervised editing and strong fixed editors, remains useful after direct target-agent training, transfers to unseen target models and tasks, and which lifecycle positions drive the gains.</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarks.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">WebShop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>)</cite> evaluates grounded web navigation: an agent must search, inspect, and purchase a product satisfying a natural-language request.
ALFWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>)</cite> is a text-based embodied environment whose household tasks require multi-step navigation, object manipulation, state tracking, and recovery.
DBBench from AgentBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>)</cite> is a relational-database environment whose natural-language tasks require schema inspection, structured SQL querying, record manipulation, and result verification.
Together, the three environments expose complementary failures in long-horizon interaction, action execution, and interface compliance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Target agents and comparisons.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our primary target is a frozen Qwen3.5-9B agent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>)</cite>.
To test whether harness adaptation remains useful after improving the actor itself, we also evaluate the same backbone after direct task-agent SFT.
Beyond this primary target, we further probe cross-model transfer by applying the trained engineer to a broad set of target agents unseen during training.
We compare the unmodified target against four groups: fixed prompt-based agentic strategies (ReAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>)</cite>, Self-Refine <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>)</cite>, and Reflection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>)</cite>); strong frontier models prompted as harness engineers (Qwen3.5-397B, GLM-5.2, Kimi-K2.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and GPT-5.5) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>)</cite>; a supervised-only engineer; and outcome-trained Harness-R1.
Within each benchmark, an editor is evaluated against the same target and task set without its generated patch.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report task success on all three benchmarks and the shaped environment score on WebShop; success is computed over 500, 500, and 300 tasks for WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench, respectively.
ALFWorld additionally reports success across its six task families and a task-level micro-average (All), and we report the average across the three benchmarks (Avg.) as the overall summary.
Reflection is reported under a separate two-episode <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{success@2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>success</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{success@2}</annotation></semantics></math> protocol: its success columns are cumulative over two episodes and its Score is measured after retrying first-episode failures, whereas all other rows report <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{success@1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>success</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{success@1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
It is therefore not ranked against single-episode methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training and selection.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The engineer is a separate 9B model initialized by cold-start SFT and then optimized with online GRPO while the target remains frozen.
The cold-start SFT set comprises roughly 1,000 executable editing examples proposed by a GPT-5.5 teacher and filtered by validation on the frozen target, and online GRPO trains on roughly 1,500 failure packets from a disjoint task split.
We select checkpoints using aggregate development performance and use the same executable patch interface for all trained variants.
Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Prompts ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> reproduces the engineer prompt template, Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> lists the training, decoding, and reward hyperparameters, and Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Data Construction and Task Splits ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> details the task-level SFT, RL, validation, and test splits.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Main Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes target-specific performance against prompt-based strategies, frontier engineers, and supervised engineer training.
We focus on task success as the primary metric.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Outcome-trained harness editing improves the frozen target.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Harness-R1 raises success on all three benchmarks and improves the equal-weight average from 44.3% to 53.6%, a gain of 9.3 percentage points.
The largest absolute gain is on ALFWorld, where success rises from 40.6% to 53.2%, while WebShop and DBBench also improve.
The outcome-trained engineer is 7.1 points above the supervised-only engineer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">A dedicated trained engineer is more effective than fixed alternatives.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Among frontier engineers, the strongest is GLM-5.2 at a 48.8% average, below Harness-R1 at 53.6%.
Prompt-based strategies are not uniformly beneficial: ReAct improves the average by 3.2 points, whereas Self-Refine reduces it by 2.5 points.
Reflection reaches 55.8% cumulative success under its two-episode protocol, which is not directly comparable to the single-episode rows.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The harness engineer co-evolves with the target agent.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Direct agent SFT raises the unmodified target to a 59.2% average, and a target-specific Harness-R1 engineer trained for this stronger actor raises it further to 64.2%, an additional 5.0 points.
Harness editing therefore keeps improving the target even after the actor itself has been fine-tuned, showing that the engineer can co-evolve with the target agent rather than saturating once the agent improves.
The gain concentrates in task success, especially on ALFWorld; although a few individual metrics dip slightly, Harness-R1 still improves the overall success of the fine-tuned agent.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Generalization across Target Agents</h3>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:44%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.02276v1/FIG_generalization_singlecol.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" width="200" height="232"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Target-agent generalization in success-rate points; Avg. weights benchmarks equally.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next ask whether the learned editing policy can adapt to target models unseen during training.
Each target supplies its own failure traces and receives a newly generated patch, so this experiment tests editor-policy transfer rather than replaying a fixed patch.
Across twenty unseen target configurations, the benchmark-averaged gain is 7.06 percentage points, and every target-level average is positive.
Across the full 21-target matrix, 56 of 63 target–benchmark combinations improve, four are unchanged, and the three regressions are all small (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 2.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mn>2.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 2.0</annotation></semantics></math> points; Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Generalization across Target Agents ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
Aggregating matched tasks within each benchmark, gains stay positive at 4.15 points on WebShop, 9.63 on ALFWorld, and 7.37 on DBBench, with every delta computed on a matched target-specific task set.
The learned editing policy thus generalizes strongly: a single training recipe transfers to targets of different families and scales, improving every one without any per-target retuning.
Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Target-Agent Generalization ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a> reports the per-target success rates before and after patch installation that underlie these deltas.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Held-Out Task Generalization</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We test whether sparse failures yield patches that improve unseen tasks.
For each benchmark and seed, every engineer observes the same 10 failures from the frozen Qwen3.5-9B target, generates one benchmark-specific patch, and applies it to all other tasks.
The pooled held-out set contains 1,270 tasks across WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench; we repeat the protocol over three matched seeds.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4.sf1" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Held-Out Task Generalization ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(a)</span></a> shows that Harness-R1 improves pooled held-out success by <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8.9\pm 1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8.9</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>1.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8.9\pm 1.5</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points and is positive for all three seeds.
Under the same protocol, Qwen3.5-397B and DeepSeek-V4-Pro yield <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-4.3\pm 2.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4.3</mn></mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>2.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-4.3\pm 2.5</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.4\pm 3.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>3.6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.4\pm 3.6</annotation></semantics></math> points, respectively.
The gap is not only in the mean: both frontier engineers straddle zero across seeds (spreads of <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 2.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>2.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 2.5</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 3.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>3.6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 3.6</annotation></semantics></math> points around negative averages), swinging between marginal gains and sizable regressions, whereas Harness-R1 stays positive on every seed at a tighter <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 1.5</annotation></semantics></math>.
Converting a handful of failures into a broadly useful edit is thus a capability that scale alone does not confer, and one that outcome-grounded training makes both stronger and more consistent.
Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Held-Out Task Generalization ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> additionally reports how many seed-benchmark patches installed a real intervention and the corresponding full-split changes.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Where in the Lifecycle Do Modifications Matter?</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Which intervention points account for the improvement?
Figure <a href="#S4.F4.sf2" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Held-Out Task Generalization ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(b)</span></a> holds the frozen target and generated patches fixed, then disables one lifecycle position at a time alongside no-intervention and full-patch controls.
The no-intervention, full-patch, and leave-one-position-out arms each rerun the target three times per benchmark and use the same equal-benchmark weighting as Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
Whiskers are standard deviations across benchmark recombinations.
The full patch reaches 53.1% average success, 8.9 points above no intervention.
Removing pre-action mediation or post-feedback recovery reduces success by 3.9 and 3.3 points, whereas removing episode-start or pre-decision changes costs 0.9 and 0.6 points.
The dominant position depends on the environment: pre-action mediation matters most on WebShop, while post-feedback recovery matters most on ALFWorld.
Because a patch can coordinate multiple positions, and the evaluated WebShop patches contain only pre-action edits, these effects are conditional and should not be added into a universal importance ranking.
Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Lifecycle-Position Ablation ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a> tabulates the per-benchmark success rates behind this ablation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para"><span id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_ERROR undefined">\FloatBarrier</span>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As agents begin to improve other agents, harness editing becomes a form of AI improving AI.
In this setting, producing edits that merely look correct is not enough: an edit intervenes directly in a running executable system, so it must be precise, verifiable, and genuinely beneficial to the agent it modifies.
This is why Harness-R1 learns from the realized task outcome of each patch rather than from whether its text appears reasonable.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training a dedicated engineer beats prompting a larger model.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in the introduction, prompting strong but fixed frontier models to edit the harness is unreliable: they optimize for plausibility, emitting syntactically valid and reasonable-looking edits, but because they never rerun the target they cannot tell whether an edit actually raises task success, so their gains are unstable and sometimes even lower reward.
Harness-R1 instead trains on the realized rerun outcome of each patch and learns edits that are genuinely useful rather than merely plausible: a valid, well-formed patch is necessary but not sufficient, and what ultimately matters is whether rerunning the target confirms a task gain.
Because the signal comes from outcomes rather than model scale, a 9B engineer trained this way surpasses much larger frontier editors (GLM-5.2 at 48.8% versus Harness-R1 at 53.6%).
Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Qualitative Case Studies ‣ Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a> inspects stored patches together with their runtime traces, including a frontier-editor patch whose plausible diagnosis compiles into behavior that lowers success.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Failure-conditioned learning beats fixed harness patterns.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fixed, hand-designed harness strategies such as Self-Refine, Reflection, and ReAct are often assumed to help agents in general, yet they apply one hand-crafted rule uniformly to every task, ignoring both the specific target’s failure modes and whether a given intervention actually works.
Our results show this is not reliable: a fixed Self-Refine rule lowers reward on all three benchmarks (an average of 2.6 points), and ReAct yields only limited and inconsistent gains.
Harness-R1 instead generates edits conditioned on the target agent’s observed failures and keeps only patches verified to help by rerun, so its improvements adapt to each target rather than betting on a single universal recipe.
This adaptivity also appears across the lifecycle: the dominant intervention point varies by environment (pre-action mediation on WebShop, post-feedback recovery on ALFWorld), which a fixed strategy cannot select on its own.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Limitations and future work.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we study a single adaptation from a vanilla target to a fine-tuned one, where a re-trained engineer still improves the stronger actor.
A natural extension is to iterate this into multi-round co-evolution that alternates updates to the target agent and the harness engineer, so that gains in one continually reshape the training signal for the other; how such alternation converges and whether it yields compounding gains is a promising path toward agents that keep improving after deployment.
Our reward is also computed from same-batch task outcomes, which keeps training grounded but ties the signal to the tasks used to mine failures.
Future work can enrich this reward with held-out performance, so that edits are explicitly optimized against regressions on unseen tasks, and with inference-efficiency terms, so that useful patches are not obtained at unnecessary runtime cost, letting a single engineer jointly balance utility, robustness, and cost.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we formalize failure-conditioned, lifecycle-wide editing of an executable agent harness as an online reinforcement learning problem for a dedicated engineer, while keeping the target agent frozen.
We propose Harness-R1, which initializes this editing policy with cold-start supervised fine-tuning and then trains it online with GRPO, so that edits are optimized for the realized task utility of executable runtime patches rather than produced by a fixed editor.
Across WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench, Harness-R1 improves every benchmark and raises the average success of the vanilla Qwen3.5-9B target from 44.3% to 53.6% (<math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+9.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>9.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+9.3</annotation></semantics></math> points), while an engineer retrained for a directly fine-tuned target further raises it from 59.2% to 64.2% (<math id="S6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+5.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>5.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+5.0</annotation></semantics></math> points).
The learned editor also generalizes: it transfers to twenty unseen target models with a positive gain on every one and improves 1,270 held-out tasks.
Together, these results show that harness construction is a learnable capability that complements weight updates and lets the engineer and target co-evolve.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Prompts</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section presents the model-facing prompt template used to train and
evaluate the harness engineer. Following the presentation style of prompt
appendices, fixed instructions are shown separately from the per-example
input. Angle-bracketed strings denote substituted fields rather than literal
tokens. SFT and online GRPO use the same response protocol; the latter
constructs the failure packet from the current frozen target-agent rollouts.
The released SFT JSON contains the complete materialized messages for all
three benchmarks.</p>
</div>

The chat template
prefills the opening <span id="A1.SS3.p2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;think&gt;</span> token sequence; training targets contain
the remaining analysis and exactly one executable patch.</span></span></p>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Implementation Details</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Cold-start SFT, online GRPO, and direct target-agent SFT each run on a single
node with eight NVIDIA H800 GPUs. The tables below list the settings needed to
reproduce each stage; framework defaults and settings that only affect memory
use, such as gradient checkpointing and the ZeRO stage, are omitted.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Harness-Engineer Cold-Start SFT</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-5.5 generates candidate patches from failure packets in the SFT task
split. We retain candidates that are executable, complete the same-batch
rerun, and achieve a non-negative task-reward change. This produces
approximately 1K teacher-filtered editing examples (877 in total: 381
WebShop, 248 ALFWorld, and 248 DBBench).</p>
</div>
